blocks.text: A container lives exactly as long as its PID 1; its state records where it is between create and removal.

blocks.src: generate: State machine: created → running (start); running ↔ paused (pause/unpause); running → exited (process ends, stop, kill); exited → running (start or restart policy); running ↔ restarting; created/exited → removed (rm); failed removal → dead
blocks.caption: Container lifecycle states.

rows: Configured, never started (or failed before exec: bad mount, port conflict)
Frozen via cgroup freezer; memory kept; no signals delivered
Restart policy between attempts, with backoff
PID 1 ended; exit code, logs and writable layer kept until rm
Removal partially failed (busy mount, storage driver)

blocks.text:
$ docker ps -a --filter status=exited
$ docker inspect -f '{{.State.Status}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}} oom={{.State.OOMKilled}}' api

items: `docker start` reuses the same container and config; `docker run` always creates a new one.
A CMD that daemonizes and returns makes the container exit immediately.
Paused isn't stopped: peers see a hung service.
Exited containers keep their name reserved and consume disk.

blocks.text: Q: "Why does my container exit right after starting?" A: "Because PID 1 ended: the command finished, the process forked into the background, or it crashed at startup. Check docker logs and .State.ExitCode, and run the main process in the foreground."

items: Paused keeps memory and blocks signals.
Exited containers keep logs until removed.
